verdict: OK to lend in Mysuru silk weaving and sarees, but only to weaver-retailers with own working capital and verified local sales; avoid units whose cash depends on KSIC's strike-hit showroom chain.
title: Mysuru silk weaving & sarees: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**A Mysuru silk unit buys raw silk and zari, weaves or gets woven sarees, and sells through showrooms and local buyers; cash comes back only when the saree sells.** KSIC's own filature at T. Narsipura runs 250 kg of raw silk a day, feeding weaving units in Mysuru and Channapatna [2]. So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower buys yarn on cash or credit and who actually holds the finished saree stock; if the stock sits in a third-party showroom, ask for the consignment agreement and the last six months of stock statements.

## Where value and cash sit
**Value sits in the saree, not the loom, and the working-capital cycle is the whole credit story.** Rating methodology flags weaving as fixed-capital and working-capital intensive, with inventory holding and receivables driving the working-capital need [8][9]. So when a proposal lands, check inventory days and receivable days against the borrower's own prior year; if inventory days are rising while sales are flat, ask which designs are not moving and at what discount they will be cleared.

## What has broken now
**KSIC, the anchor brand, is disrupted: all 1,052 employees of its three units stopped production and all 13 showrooms ran with empty racks [3].** Separately, the government has discussed stopping online sale of Mysuru silk sarees in favour of local sale [1]. Both items are local news from February-March 2026 and may have moved since; collect from customer the current KSIC supply position. Peer Sai Silks reported Q1 FY2027 revenue flat at INR 375 crore with same-store sales down 7.5%-7.8% [4], and Siyaram saw occasion-driven demand with moderate footfall in Q3 FY2026 [7]. So when a proposal lands, check how much of the borrower's sales went to KSIC or its showrooms; if it is a large share, ask for the replacement buyer and the credit terms.

## Where to grow
**Karnataka is running ahead of India: GST collections up 11.1% Apr-to-date against 6.1% nationally, and electricity demand up 23.3% against 9.5% [D].** Pursue weaver-retailers with their own showroom, wedding-season order books and a second buyer channel; Sai Silks names Karnataka as the front lead in its expansion [6]. Avoid pure job-work units with one buyer and no stock of their own.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the inventory, not the loom.** Take monthly stock and receivable statements, a quarterly sales register by channel, and annual GST returns; covenant that inventory days and receivable days stay within the sanction note. Rating reports stress that low leverage and longer-tenure term debt protect coverage [10], and that TUFS interest subsidy runs seven years from sanction [10]. So price term loans to the subsidy tenure; if the borrower wants a longer tenor, ask for the repayment source beyond the subsidy.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the buyer mix and the stock, not the order book.** A rising share of sales to KSIC-linked channels, discount-led clearing of old designs, or stock statements that stop matching showroom sales are the first signals. Collect from customer the monthly sales by channel and the age-wise stock; if either slips for two months, ask for the buyer-wise ledger before renewing.
watch: Inventory days rise two months running -> ask for age-wise stock and design-wise discount
KSIC-linked share crosses the sanctioned limit -> seek replacement buyer and revise limit
Turnover falls below the sanctioned projection -> reprice or reduce limit
Leverage rises above the sanction note -> require promoter infusion before renewal
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
